newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish politician shot by ETA dies, clashes erupt.
newsitem.headline: Spanish politician shot by ETA dies, clashes erupt.

text.p: A young Spanish politician kidnapped and shot by ETA Basque guerrillas died of his wounds on Sunday, sparking a violent backlash against the radical separatist group and international condemnation.
The Pope denounced the killing as an "act of blood".

Fierce clashes between supporters and opponents of ETA erupted in the northern city of Pamplona on Sunday morning hours after hospital officials announced 29-year-old Miguel Angel Blanco had died of two gunshot wounds to the head.
Police fired rubber bullets to break up the confrontations.

The guerrillas abducted Blanco on Thursday afternoon and killed him two days later after the government refused its demand to transfer about 500 ETA inmates scattered throughout the country to prisons in the autonomous Basque region.

Blanco, a low-ranking member of Spain's ruling party, was found bound and bleeding on a roadside shortly after the 4 p.m. deadline on Saturday. Just before dawn on Sunday, the 29-year-old Basque town councillor was declared "clinically brain dead", said Doctor Garcia Urra, of the San Sebastian hospital's intensive care unit.
The news of Blanco's death before dawn on Sunday hit members of his family hard. "There was a very strong reaction, above all from the mother, sister and girlfriend," Urra said.
The family had already had to endure an earlier mistaken announcement that he was dead.
Pope John Paul on Sunday condemned the murder as an unjustifiable act of barbarity.

"I have followed with pain the news from Spain about the barbarous assassination of young Spanish politician Miguel Angel Blanco," he told followers. "I forcefully deplore this act of blood. The killing of an innocent victim can never have justification."

Blanco's ordeal, which was also condemned by France, touched a raw nerve among Spaniards, who in recent months have faced a growing wave of violence by the rebels. ETA has killed nearly 800 people in its 29-year fight for independence.
More than a million Spaniards showed their outrage at the kidnapping in a series of massive peaceful demonstrations across the country on Friday and Saturday, but the kidnappers took no notice.
The largest was led by Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar in the Basque city of Bilbao where half a million people turned out to demand Blanco's release hours before the deadline expired.

The anger turned to violence on Sunday morning when hundreds of Spanish youths shouting "Sons of Bitches" and "Murderers" attacked a handful of ETA sympathisers in the northern Spanish city of Pamplona.
They tried to burn the local headquarters of the separatist group's political wing, Herri Batasuna.
The rival groups threw bottles and rocks at each other. Police in riot gear with their faces masked tried to break up the clashes.

When the demonstrators tried to storm Herri Batasuna's headquarters, police opened fire with rubber bullets. They also kicked protesters and used batons to beat them back. A number of people were bleeding and bruised in the clashes, witnesses said.
Police also stopped the youths from burning a bar where Herri Batasuna members meet in Pamplona.

When the clashes erupted, Pamplona was packed with tens of thousands of visitors celebrating the world-famous running of the bulls festival that began one week ago. Most of the youths involved in the violence were dressed in the traditional fiesta white costume with red headbands and sashes.
The annual fiesta in northern Spain was suspended from Saturday night to Sunday night to show "sadness and indignation" over Blanco's abduction and shooting.
In the first official reaction to Blanco's death, an Interior Ministry spokesman said Herri Batasuna would suffer the consequences of the killing.

"The first is Herri Batasuna and its universe must feel the pressure of the whole society which does not tolerate people who do not condemn this type of unjustified barbarity," spokesman Cayetano Gonzalez said.

Blanco was the 10th person killed by ETA so far this year. The group had kidnapped 77 people in its history and set deadlines to execute hostages only twice before. In both previous cases, the threat was carried out.
The front pages of Spain's Sunday newspapers reflected the angry mood. "Sons of Bitches," declared a headline in Diario 16. "Beasts!" said another in the newspaper YA.
Basque political parties planned to meet on Sunday to discuss a response to ETA's action. The government called a meeting of a multi-party anti-terrorist group on Monday.
